name: Chad
card_headline: Chad freed opposition leader Masra under a pardon that keeps his conviction, while Sudan's war, Boko Haram and army rifts press on a president with no term limit.
card_summary: President Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno now holds a seven-year term with no limit on renewal. Opposition leader Succès Masra left prison in August under a pardon, but HRW says his conviction stands and he cannot run. Chad hosts about 1.5 million refugees, mostly Sudanese, and drone strikes from Sudan have hit Tine. Boko Haram killed at least 23 soldiers in May. Chad is leaving the ICC and is rebuilding military ties with France.
card_local: Tchadinfos reported Masra's release on 14 August and his call for reconciliation, and Alwihda Info reported the president sacking officials in Ennedi Ouest in November. [1][2]
card_international: Al Jazeera, AFP, Reuters and AP report the ICC withdrawal, the drone strike on Tine and the Boko Haram attacks. [3][4][5]
card_scholar: ISS sees signs of a renewed French military partnership, and the Africa Center warns that security forces built on loyalty networks raise coup risk. [6][7]
context_md: Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno took power in 2021 after his father, Idriss Déby, died fighting rebels in the north. [8] On 20 October 2022, security forces killed more than 50 protesters who opposed an extension of the transition, according to Crisis Group. [8] In the 2024 presidential election the official result gave Déby 61.3 percent and Masra 18.5 percent, and Masra claimed victory. [9] Opposition figure Yaya Dillo died in a 2024 raid on his party's headquarters. [10] Chad ended its defence pact with France in November 2024. [6] Constitutional amendments promulgated in October 2025 set a seven-year presidential term with no limit on renewal. [11] More than 918,000 people have fled Sudan to eastern Chad since April 2023. [12]

sections.title: A pardon freed Masra, but his conviction, his ban from office and the 2025 term-limit change all stand
sections.body_md:
Succès Masra, the former prime minister who ran against President Déby in 2024, was arrested on 16 May 2025 after clashes in Mandakao and convicted on 9 August 2025 of inciting hatred and violence. [10][13] He received 20 years and a fine of 1 billion CFA francs, about US$1.8 million. [10] He pleaded not guilty, and the Supreme Court upheld the sentence in May 2026. [13][9] On the evening of 14 August 2026 a presidential pardon freed him, together with eight leaders of the opposition coalition GCAP. [1][13] HRW dates the release to 15 August. [13]

The pardon decree described the releases as a step toward national unity and reconciliation, HRW says. HRW adds that the convictions, the fines and the criminal record remain, that Masra is still barred from running for office, and that 65 of his co-defendants stay in prison, a figure that may include people who died in detention, which HRW could not confirm. [13] Speaking to supporters, Masra thanked the president, said he is innocent, urged them not to seek revenge and said he is ready to work with the president and other political forces. [1]

The rules on power have also changed. Parliament approved amendments in late 2025 that raise the presidential term from five to seven years and remove any limit on re-election. [14] The Chadian journalist Nathan Leubnoudji Tah writes that the president promulgated the text on 8 October 2025 without public consultation, and that it lets the president lead a party. [11] Africanews reports 236 of 257 lawmakers in favour, with some opposition members boycotting, while HRW gives a National Assembly tally of 171 in favour, one abstention and none against. [14][10] Opposition leader Albert Pahimi Padacké called the change unconstitutional and authoritarian. [14] Tah argues that the 'technical revision' label, which needs only a three-fifths majority and no referendum, covers changes to nearly the whole text. [11]

lenses.local: Tchadinfos reported Masra's release, his claim of innocence and his offer to work with the president. [1]
lenses.international: HRW, AFP and Africanews document the sentence, the failed appeal and the limits of the pardon. [13][9]
lenses.scholar: Tah's ConstitutionNet essay compares the term-limit change with 2005, when similar changes preceded a rebel uprising. [11]

sections.title: The opposition coalition is dissolved, journalists face charges and Chad is leaving the ICC
sections.body_md:
On 25 April 2026 nine leaders of GCAP, a coalition of 13 parties, were arrested after the Ministry of Public Security banned a march planned for 2 May and dissolved the coalition. The government cited a risk to public order and a Supreme Court decision, according to allAfrica, which attributes the arrest details to Africa Radio. [15] HRW says the Supreme Court dissolved GCAP in April and that eight leaders received eight-year sentences for rebellion linked to planning a protest march. [13] UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the UN was concerned about the arrests and called for due process. [16] Africanews, citing AFP, reports that police shot dead a member of Masra's party at a protest in late April, and that several journalists were refused entry to his Supreme Court hearing. [9]

RSF ranked Chad 93rd of 180 in its 2026 index, up from 108th, and still calls the situation problematic, citing pressure on journalists, self-censorship and limited access to information. [17] HRW records that the journalists Olivier Monodji and Mahamat Saleh Alhissein were arrested in March 2025 and charged with espionage and endangering state security, allegedly over Wagner Group coverage, and were held without trial until July. In September 2025 the blogger Makaila Nguebla and the activist-journalist Charfadine Galmaye Saleh were stripped of their nationality; both are in exile. [10]

On 27 July 2026 Chad began withdrawing from the International Criminal Court, the fifth state to do so in recent months. Its government called the court's record uneven and criticised its focus on Africa, and said a senior US diplomat had phoned to urge it to reconsider its membership, according to AFP and Reuters. [3][18] The Assembly of States Parties urged Chad and Venezuela on 7 August to reverse course. [18] Lawyers for Othman Dillo, a brother of Yaya Dillo, say the withdrawal takes effect in July 2027 and plan to go to the court. They accuse the new foreign minister of involvement in Yaya Dillo's February 2024 death, which the government describes as an exchange of fire. [19]

lenses.local: Tchadinfos carried the UN's concern about the arrests and the Wadi Fira killings, and reported RSF's index. [16][17]
lenses.international: HRW, AFP, Reuters and Africanews cover the dissolution, the sentences and the ICC move. [13][3][9]

sections.title: The Sudan war has reached Chad's border towns, and N'Djamena's links to the UAE are contested
sections.body_md:
Chad closed its border with Sudan on 23 February 2026 to stop the conflict spreading. A rocket from Sudan hit Tine in late February, and one tally cited by AFP-style wire copy counts 23 deaths in Tine since late December: 15 soldiers and eight civilians. [4] On 18 March a drone strike on Tine killed 17 people, the Chadian government said. The RSF denied involvement and blamed the Sudanese army, which said the drone was the RSF's, and the article does not confirm who launched it. [4] A European asylum agency briefing based on ACLED data says reports put the toll at 19. [20] President Déby ordered the army to retaliate against attacks from Sudan. [4]

MSF says that since early February it and Chad's health ministry treated 457 injured people in Tine, responded to 13 mass-casualty incidents and saw 38 deaths in two hospitals. It closed its Mabrouka hospital near the border on 21 February because of shelling. [21]

Whether N'Djamena helps the RSF is disputed. Chad and the UAE deny it, according to Crisis Group as relayed by Al Jazeera's Arabic service. [19] In October 2024 Chad's government spokesman Abderaman Koulamallah called such reports fanciful while acknowledging good relations with the UAE. His accuser was Minni Minnawi, who leads a Darfur faction allied with Khartoum, and a US-funded Sudan Conflict Observatory report had alleged UAE supply through Amdjarass airport. [22] ISS says a UN report suggests the UAE could use Chad's bases to move equipment to the RSF. [6] A summary of a November 2024 Crisis Group report says Chadian officials tacitly allowed the routing of weapons. [23] The Africa Center researcher Bourdjolbo Tchoudiba writes that the government likely supports the RSF for financial, security and geopolitical reasons, and counts $200 million of UAE financing in 2023 plus a $500 million loan in October 2024, about 15 percent of the annual budget. [7] None of this was independently confirmed in the sources read for this draft.

lenses.international: Dawn and MSF document the strikes on Tine and the toll on the town's hospitals. [4][21]
lenses.scholar: The Africa Center and a Crisis Group summary treat Chad's UAE ties as a risk to its claimed neutrality. [7][23]

sections.title: Chad hosts about 1.5 million refugees on a response that is about a fifth funded
sections.body_md:
UNHCR counted about 1.5 million refugees in Chad at the end of 2025, about 1.3 million of them Sudanese, and 183,000 new arrivals from Sudan during that year. [24] UNICEF counts more than 918,000 people who fled Sudan to eastern Chad since April 2023 and expects the refugee population to reach 1.48 million by December 2026. [12] Al Jazeera reports that UNHCR saw arrivals accelerate in September to about 400 a day, roughly 20 times the earlier rate, and that more than 55,000 had arrived so far in 2026 through Adre and Tine. The Tine transit centre held over 4,300 people, most refugees got less than half the minimum daily water, and the UN had received 20 percent of a $1.6 billion appeal. [25]

UNHCR's own 2025 report says its $409.1 million Chad budget was 37.5 percent funded, cites a sudden US funding reduction, and says cuts forced three office closures and a staff reduction of about 20 percent. It also records that 84 percent of refugees live below the national poverty line. [24]

The Timbuktu Institute, summarising the 2026 response plan, says about 4.5 million people in Chad need help, that the plan targets 3.4 million at an estimated $986.1 million, and that the government and the UN signed a memorandum on 2 September to strengthen state-led aid coordination. [26] FEWS NET expected Crisis (IPC phase 3) outcomes in parts of the east and in Lac province through September 2026 and put Emergency (phase 4) below 15 percent of the population. It counts imported rice 62 percent above its five-year average and fuel prices up more than 40 percent during 2025. [27]

lenses.international: Al Jazeera, citing UNHCR, reports a sharp rise in arrivals and a funding gap. [25]
lenses.scholar: FEWS NET, UNHCR and the Timbuktu Institute provide the figures on food, funding and needs. [27][24][26]

sections.title: Boko Haram in the west, water feuds in the east and a gold dispute in the north stretch the army
sections.body_md:
ACLED data compiled in a June 2026 European asylum agency briefing record 184 violent incidents in Chad between January 2025 and March 2026, with 349 victims, at least 223 of them civilians. The UN counts about 200 civilian deaths from intercommunal conflict in 2025 and about 100 from jihadist violence, and the briefing says ACLED's method probably undercounts. [20]

On the night of 4 May 2026 an attack on a military post on Barka Tolorom island in the Lake Chad region killed at least 23 Chadian soldiers and wounded 26, according to the army, which attributes it to Boko Haram. The president called the attack cowardly. [5] Al Jazeera and AFP report a further ambush on 6 May that killed two generals, and three days of national mourning. They add that the army had claimed in February 2025 that Boko Haram had no more sanctuary in Chad, but attacks on security forces continued. [28] The asylum agency says two factions, JAS and ISWAP, remain active and recruit locally, and that about 243,000 internally displaced people live in the region. [20]

In Wadi Fira, a dispute between two families over water in the village of Igote escalated from 25 April and killed at least 42 people, according to Deputy Prime Minister Limane Mahamat, who said the army intervened and that mediation and judicial proceedings had begun. [29] In the gold-producing north, two officers of a mining brigade were killed and nine wounded in Miski on 14 October. The army says the attackers belong to the local self-defence committee and four people are under arrest; this rests on one outlet relaying army statements. [30]

On 7 November the president began a security tour of several provinces. In Ennedi Ouest he removed two prefects and a sub-prefect, demoted and suspended the commander of defence zone 8, and ordered civilians disarmed, after a government delegate warned that a dispute over pasture and water risked open confrontation. [2]

lenses.local: Alwihda Info reports the president's sanctions in Ennedi Ouest, drawing on the presidency and a government delegate. [2]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera, AFP and AP carry the Boko Haram attacks and the Wadi Fira toll. [5][28][29]
lenses.scholar: The asylum agency's ACLED-based briefing is the best regional breakdown found. [20]

sections.title: Rifts in the army and a cousin's coup threat sit beside a quiet return of French forces
sections.body_md:
Al Jazeera's Arabic service, relaying Africa Intelligence and Le Monde on 29 September, reports that General Othman Dillo, a cousin of the president, said at a Paris press conference earlier that month that he would return to overthrow him. These are Dillo's claims and the outlets' reporting, and the government's reply is not in the article. [19] Africa Intelligence reports that Déby dismissed about 10 Zaghawa officers in April 2025 and that two elite units, the presidential guard and a rapid intervention force formed in 2023, are rivals. Crisis Group's Enrica Picco says the violence is deepening splits in the ruling elite, and Crisis Group said in July that Déby's grip could weaken, though no Zaghawa figure now has the support to challenge him. [19] Tchoudiba writes that Chad's security forces rely on loyalty networks rather than institutions, which raises the risk of coups and rebel realignments. [7]

On 21 September 2026 Déby named General Ahmat Kogri, a former head of the national security agency ANSE, as foreign minister in place of Abdoulaye Sabre Fadoul. [31] Dillo's lawyers filed a complaint in Paris in June 2025 accusing Kogri of involvement in the February 2024 killing of Yaya Dillo. No investigation has been opened in France and Kogri has not been charged. [19]

ISS's Remadji Hoinathy writes that since March 2026 signs point to a renewed French military partnership, with a liaison detachment of about 600 troops, down from about 2,300. [6] He says an attempted partnership with Russia did not succeed, and that Türkiye supplied armoured vehicles and drones and Hungary signed cooperation agreements. [6] The Timbuktu Institute says ties with Moscow have grown, with a new Russian ambassador sworn in on 3 September. It adds that after a mutiny in Niamey on 28 and 29 August, a Nigerien officer claimed on state television that Chadian officials helped prepare an intervention. N'Djamena called the claim ridiculous, and the institute says no material evidence backs it. [26]

Chad is also a troop contributor abroad. Déby told lawmakers in April that Chad would send 1,500 troops to Haiti in two battalions of 750 for one year, and that 400 had already gone. [32] The Gang Suppression Force described the Chadian advance team as its first troop deployment on 1 April. [33]

lenses.local: Tchadinfos reports Kogri's appointment by decree on 21 September and his earlier post as head of ANSE. [31]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and AP report the coup threat, the Haiti deployment and the rifts in the army. [19][32]
lenses.scholar: ISS and the Africa Center treat France's return and the loyalty-based security forces as the main strategic questions. [6][7]

sections.title: Growth is above 5 percent on paper, but oil revenue, power cuts and prices leave households exposed
sections.body_md:
The IMF Executive Board approved a 48-month Extended Credit Facility for Chad on 25 July 2025, worth SDR 455.65 million, about US$655 million. After a November 2025 mission, IMF staff said real GDP grew 5.0 percent in 2024, raised the 2026 growth forecast to 5.1 percent from 3.6 percent, and said inflation was negative 4.3 percent in November 2025 as food prices fell from record highs. [34] Quantitative targets at end-June 2025 were met, but a net domestic financing target was missed because bank restructuring was delayed, reforms on VAT credits and banks are behind schedule, and oil revenue came in below projections, mainly because the US dollar fell. The staff-level agreement still needed IMF Board approval at the time of the release. [34]

Households face other pressures. FEWS NET counts fuel prices up more than 40 percent during 2025, imported rice 62 percent above its five-year average and more than 100 percent above in several eastern markets, and millet 13 percent below its five-year average. It warns that the Middle East conflict could raise transport and import costs and cut remittances from the Gulf. [27] UNHCR says 84 percent of refugees in Chad live below the national poverty line. [24]

Tchadinfos reported during the president's 11 and 12 November visit to Abéché that the city's solar power plant has been shut for nine months and a mother and child hospital has been stalled since 2015, without naming a source. A government delegate said 330 gold traders' shops will be built with the traders' own funds. [35] Tchoudiba counts about $700 million of UAE financing since 2023, roughly 15 percent of the annual budget. [7] The IMF page read for this draft gives no public debt figures.

lenses.local: Tchadinfos reports the stalled Abéché solar plant and hospital during the president's tour. [35]
lenses.scholar: FEWS NET and the Africa Center supply the price and external-financing figures. [27][7]

reporters.name: Daniel Khalili-Tari
reporters.bio: Wrote the 25 September 2026 Al Jazeera report on more than 55,000 Sudanese refugees reaching Chad this year.
reporters.why: The report puts UNHCR arrival figures, shelter and water shortages and the funding gap in one place.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Remadji Hoinathy
reporters.role: Senior researcher, Institute for Security Studies
reporters.bio: Wrote the 19 August 2026 ISS Today analysis of Chad's renewed military ties with France.
reporters.why: Sets France, the UAE, Türkiye, Russia and Hungary side by side as Chad's security partners.
reporters.label: ISS Africa

reporters.name: Nathan Leubnoudji Tah
reporters.role: Publishing director, Le Mirador; vice-president, Union of Chadian Journalists
reporters.bio: Wrote the 4 November 2025 ConstitutionNet essay on the October 2025 constitutional amendments.
reporters.why: A Chadian journalist's clause-by-clause account of what changed and how it passed.
reporters.label: ConstitutionNet

reporters.name: Lewis Mudge
reporters.role: Central Africa director, Human Rights Watch
reporters.bio: Quoted in HRW's 21 August 2026 release calling for Masra's conviction to be set aside.
reporters.why: HRW's main voice on the Masra case and the wider crackdown on opponents.
reporters.label: Human Rights Watch

reporters.name: Enrica Picco
reporters.role: Central Africa director, International Crisis Group
reporters.bio: Guest on Crisis Group's October 2022 podcast on the crackdown in Chad, and cited in September 2026 on splits in the ruling elite.
reporters.why: Crisis Group's analyst on Chad's elite and army, quoted on the risk the Sudan war poses to the ruling circle.
reporters.label: Crisis Group, Hold Your Fire

reporters.name: Bourdjolbo Tchoudiba
reporters.role: Researcher, Laboratoire Hannah Arendt (LIPHA) and Centre d'Études Africaines de Cluj-Napoca
reporters.bio: Author of the Africa Center for Strategic Studies analysis of how the Sudan conflict threatens Chad's stability.
reporters.why: Gives financing figures for UAE support and a case for active neutrality. The Arabic Al Jazeera piece spells the first name Borgoulbo.
reporters.label: Africa Center for Strategic Studies

reporters.name: Marielle Debos
reporters.role: Author, Living by the Gun in Chad
reporters.bio: Wrote the 2016 Zed Books study based on more than ten years of fieldwork in Chad.
reporters.why: The standard English-language study of how fighters live between wars and how impunity shapes the state.
reporters.label: Blackwell's

reporters.name: Olivier Monodji
reporters.bio: HRW reports he was arrested in March 2025 with Mahamat Saleh Alhissein, charged with espionage and endangering state security, held without trial and released in July.
reporters.why: His case is the clearest recent example of the risk to Chadian reporters who cover the Wagner Group and security matters.
reporters.label: Human Rights Watch

books.title: Living by the Gun in Chad: Combatants, Impunity and State Formation
books.author: Marielle Debos
books.why: Based on more than ten years of fieldwork, it argues that armed violence has become a livelihood and a political language in Chad.
books.label: Blackwell's

books.author: Ésaïe Toïngar
books.why: A hostile account of the late president's rule and his role in the Darfur wars. Its allegations are the author's own and should be read as an argument.

books.author: Mario Azevedo
books.why: Examines Chad's socioeconomic and political history and challenges common myths about it, as background for the present.
books.label: WorldCat

books.author: Jérôme Tubiana and Marielle Debos
books.why: A USIP and ISS study drawing on several hundred interviews on how domestic politics shaped Chad's regional role. It is a report, not a book.
books.label: ISS Africa

scores.coverage_basis: Wire copy on Chad arrives when something breaks: the Boko Haram attack in May, the Tine drone strike in March and the ICC withdrawal in July [5][4][3]. Chadian outlets cover domestic politics in French, and think tanks such as ISS and the Africa Center publish steadily, but the refugee crisis gets far less attention than Sudan itself [1][6][7].

severity.basis: ACLED recorded 184 violent incidents between January 2025 and March 2026, and Boko Haram killed at least 23 soldiers on 4 May 2026 [20][5]. Drone strikes from Sudan hit Tine in March [4].
About 1.5 million refugees and about 4.5 million people in need, with the UN response about a fifth funded [24][26][25].
Masra was freed by pardon but remains convicted and barred, GCAP was dissolved, and the presidential term limit was removed [13][15][14].

Growth was 5.0 percent in 2024 under an IMF programme, but oil revenue is below projections, fuel prices rose over 40 percent in 2025 and 84 percent of refugees live below the poverty line [34][27][24].
Cross-border strikes, army rifts and a coup threat from a presidential cousin point to rising risk, while RSF's press index improved by 15 places [19][4][17].

parts.basis: France is returning with about 600 troops, the UAE has lent Chad money and is accused of using its territory, and Russia, Türkiye and Hungary are courting N'Djamena [6][7][26].
Chad is a small oil producer under an IMF programme with limited weight in world trade [34].
The Sudan war is crossing into Chad, Boko Haram operates around Lake Chad, and a refugee wave could push people toward Libya or Europe [4][5][23].
Over 900,000 Sudanese have arrived since 2023 and UNHCR warns more may attempt the journey to Europe [12][25].
Chad is leaving the ICC at US urging and removed presidential term limits [3][14].

summary: Chad matters beyond its borders mainly as the host of Sudan's refugees, as a corridor in the Sudan war that the UAE and others are accused of using, and as a Sahel state realigning between France, Russia and Gulf backers [25][6][26]. Its trade weight is small [34].
gi.up: A coup attempt, a breakdown of the border or proof of weapons transfers to the RSF through Chad.
gi.down: A ceasefire in Sudan and steady funding for the refugee response.

gaps: Local sourcing is partial: Tchadinfos (five articles) and Alwihda Info (one) were read, but Le Mirador, Chadian radio and the government's own announcements were not. Independent press is under pressure, according to HRW and RSF.
The 2025 term-limit vote is reported with two different tallies (236 of 257 per Africanews; 171 in favour in the National Assembly per HRW), and the two were not reconciled.
Masra's release is dated 14 August by Tchadinfos and 15 August by HRW. The 2025 Mandakao toll is 42 in HRW's release and 41 in its World Report, citing the government.

The claims about General Othman Dillo, the army rifts and Kogri come from one Arabic-language Al Jazeera article relaying Africa Intelligence and Le Monde. Neither was read directly, and the government's reply was not found.
The UAE budget share (about 15 percent per the Africa Center) and the claim of more than 80 percent in a secondary Crisis Group summary conflict. The Crisis Group report itself was not opened.
The Tine toll is 17 per the Chadian government and 19 in the asylum agency briefing; responsibility for the strike is unconfirmed.
The $1.6 billion appeal in Al Jazeera's refugee report is not described by scope and differs from the $986.1 million national plan cited by the Timbuktu Institute.
The EUAA briefing was read through the first 100,000 of about 230,000 characters, so Lake Chad incident counts were not seen.
The IMF release read does not give public debt, and no World Bank 2026 poverty figure was found. Oil output and pipeline revenue were not researched.
The Miski attack and the Abéché solar plant status each rest on one Chadian or regional outlet.
No Chadian documentary or film was verified, so media is empty. Podcast episodes are older than a year (2022 and 2025) or are video interviews.

Book author for Azevedo comes from a bookseller listing title in search results; the WorldCat page did not list an author. Toïngar's book is a critical account and its allegations are not verified here.
The September 2026 constitution and electoral timetable for the next presidential election were not found, so no election date is stated.
